name: Scarcity
statement: Things in short supply, and things that have just become short, are rated as more desirable and more valuable than the same things in plentiful supply.
meaning: The claim is about how an object is valued, not about the psychology of being poor. Brock's commodity theory puts it generally, and Lynn quotes the central sentence from page 246: any commodity will be valued to the extent that it is unavailable. Marketing research splits the cue into three kinds. Supply-based scarcity restricts how many exist, demand-based scarcity signals that other buyers have taken them, and time-based scarcity closes the window for buying. The three travel under one name and do not behave alike. Reactance, which has its own entry here, is one candidate explanation for the effect rather than the effect itself.

origin.note: Brock's chapter set out commodity theory, of which the scarcity effect is the best known prediction. The demonstration usually cited is seven years later, Worchel, Lee and Adewole's cookie experiment of 1975. The route into marketing practice runs through Cialdini's Influence, which both meta-analyses below cite for the claim itself rather than for evidence.

evidence: The cookie experiment is described here from its abstract, because the paper is paywalled. Participants rated the value and attractiveness of cookies held either in abundant or in scarce supply. Supply was either constant or changing, and a change was attributed either to an accident or to demand from other participants. These conditions were crossed with what participants believed about how many more people were still to take part. Cookies in scarce supply were rated as more desirable than cookies in abundant supply. Cookies whose supply fell from abundant to scarce were rated as more valuable than cookies that had been scarce throughout, and cookies scarce through demand beat cookies scarce through an accident. The authors read the results as an extension of commodity theory and hypothesised reactance as an intervening process behind some of them. A second study was run to rule out demand characteristics. No sample size, mean or test statistic from that paper is quoted on this page. Lynn pooled the first two decades of the literature: 41 studies containing 51 tests of the scarcity principle, combined by the Stouffer method to z = 8.39. The mean effect size was r = 0.12, rising to 0.17 once five significant reversals were dropped as outliers, and individual effects ran from -0.54 to 0.43 with significant heterogeneity, chi-squared(48) = 190.22, p < 0.005. Tests of the uniqueness explanation gave a combined z = 3.59 while reaching significance in only 4 of 11 tests.

replication.headline: Two meta-analyses thirty years apart both find a positive pooled effect, and the modern one puts it at 0.31 on purchase intentions across 193 effect sizes.
replication.detail: Barton, Zlatevska and Oppewal pooled 416 effect sizes from 131 studies published over 50 years. For purchase intentions they report 193 effect sizes covering 22,655 participants at 0.31, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.37, z = 10.01. Their metric is a reliability-corrected, inverse-variance-weighted standardised mean difference rather than a plain Cohen's d. The same pooling gives attitude 0.15, desirability 0.25, enjoyment 0.33, perceived value 0.37, perceived quality 0.47, willingness to pay 0.47, exclusivity 0.52 and popularity 0.71. Ladeira and colleagues pooled 335 effect sizes from 37 articles and report a mean of 0.2776, printed with a 95% interval of 0.2243 to 0.3209, z = 11.06, with I-squared of 68% and chi-squared(224) = 875.83. The two disagree about which cue does the work. Barton found supply-based scarcity largest at 0.39, time-based at 0.34 and demand-based at 0.28, a spread that did not reach significance, Q(2) = 1.76, p = .414. Ladeira found the ordering the other way round and called it significant: excessive demand 0.5484, 95% CI 0.4412 to 0.6557, against restricted supply 0.1859, 95% CI 0.1362 to 0.2355, with a metaregression coefficient of -0.346, p < 0.001. They agree on limited quantity against limited time. Ladeira gives limited quantity 0.287 from 96 effects and limited time 0.3952 from 51, with a coefficient of 0.1030, standard error 0.0649, whose interval includes zero.

study.cite: Barton, B. L., Zlatevska, N., & Oppewal, H. (2022). Scarcity tactics in marketing: A meta-analysis of product scarcity effects on consumer purchase intentions. Journal of Retailing, 98(4), 741-758.

limits: Almost all of this is an intention recorded in a scenario. Of Barton's 193 purchase-intention effect sizes, 178 came from hypothetical manipulations and 15 from actual ones, and 152 of them came from student samples. Neither contrast reached significance, Q(1) = 0.08 for manipulation type and Q(1) = 1.56 for sample composition, so the small real-behaviour set does not contradict the rest. It is also too small to settle anything, and Barton's own list of open questions asks under what conditions purchase intentions turn into purchases. Lynn made the same complaint in 1991, writing that little research to date had used these manipulations in real-world marketing contexts. Publication bias is handled in both papers by a fail-safe count and nothing else. Barton excluded unpublished studies and reports that between 30 and 6,985 null studies would be needed to overturn the findings; Lynn's equivalent figure was 1,277. Effects differ by country in Barton's data at Q(5) = 10.33, p = .066, with Korea at 0.70 and Canada at 0.49 against Germany at 0.05 and the Netherlands at 0.19, the last two not significant. Lynn declined to interpret his own moderators, on the grounds that the study characteristics he coded were highly correlated and that different but equally defensible inclusion decisions changed the answers. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex, Europe PMC and general web search found no preregistered or multi-laboratory direct replication of the 1975 cookie experiment, so the case rests on meta-analytic accumulation of conceptual replications. The 1975 paper is paywalled at APA PsycNet and at Ovid, Unpaywall records no open copy, and its abstract was read here from the record at OpenAlex.
misreadings: The loudest confusion is with a different literature. Mullainathan and Shafir's work on the scarcity of money and time asks what having too little does to attention and decision-making, which is not a claim about what a limited edition does to a product's appeal. It carries its own contested record. O'Donnell and colleagues replicated 20 studies drawn from the papers citing a seminal publication in that field and report that four of the replications came out significant, that replication effect sizes were smaller than the originals for 80% of the 20 studies, and that they were directionally opposite for 30%. Isler, Yilmaz and Dulleck's preregistered test of the related claim that scarcity frames value, with 3,442 participants, supported it. None of those numbers describe the effect on this page. Reactance is a hypothesis about scarcity rather than a finding about it. Worchel and colleagues offered it as an intervening process behind some of their results. Barton and colleagues treat commodity theory as the dominant framework, list conformity, regret and reactance as alternatives, and say their meta-analysis could not code variables belonging to those frameworks because too few studies measured them. Lynn notes that reactance predicts a scarcity effect only where a person treats possession as a right or a freedom, which is narrower than what commodity theory claims. A third error is that limited-time appeals beat limited-quantity appeals, or the reverse. Both meta-analyses looked and found no difference worth reporting. Scarcity also does not always raise value. Five of the 51 tests in Lynn's set reversed significantly, three of them in studies where participants ranked commodities they believed would then be handed out, a setting in which naming the scarce one looks selfish. Last, the effect is smaller than the anecdotes imply. Lynn's mean r of 0.12 accounts for about 1% of the variance, which he renders as a success rate moving from 44% to 56%.

sources.text: Brock, T. C. (1968). Implications of commodity theory for value change. In Psychological Foundations of Attitudes (pp. 243-275). Academic Press. The chapter was not read; its central claim is quoted on this page from Lynn (1991).

Worchel, S., Lee, J., & Adewole, A. (1975). Effects of supply and demand on ratings of object value. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(5), 906-914. Full text paywalled; described here from the abstract carried by the OpenAlex record for this DOI.
Lynn, M. (1991). Scarcity effects on value: A quantitative review of the commodity theory literature. Psychology & Marketing, 8(1), 43-57. Read from the author copy at Cornell eCommons.

Barton, B. L., Zlatevska, N., & Oppewal, H. (2022). Scarcity tactics in marketing: A meta-analysis of product scarcity effects on consumer purchase intentions. Journal of Retailing, 98(4), 741-758. Read from the accepted version in the Bond University repository.

Ladeira, W. J., Lim, W. M., Santini, F. de O., Rasul, T., Perin, M. G., & Altinay, L. (2023). A meta-analysis on the effects of product scarcity. Psychology & Marketing, 40(7), 1267-1279. Read from the copy in the Oxford Brookes RADAR repository.

O'Donnell, M., et al. (2021). Empirical audit and review and an assessment of evidentiary value in research on the psychological consequences of scarcity. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 118(44), e2103313118. Cited for the resource-scarcity literature, which is not the effect described on this page.

Isler, O., Yilmaz, O., & Dulleck, U. (2023). Scarcity improves economic valuations when cognitively salient. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 209, 362-371. Abstract read at the Australian National University research portal; the article itself was not opened.

Cialdini, R. B. Influence. Named as the route by which scarcity reached marketing practice, cited by Lynn (1991) as the 1985 edition and by Barton and colleagues (2022) as the 2009 edition. The book was not read and no claim on this page rests on it.
